5.directions: Read the text and choose the answer (A, B, C or D) which you think fits best according to the text.
5.title: Keeping the Past Alive
5.passage:
When people talk about preserving historical heritage, they often picture famous castles, grand museums or ancient temples. Yet the task is much wider than protecting a few celebrated landmarks. In many towns, heritage can be found in ordinary streets, old workshops, local archives and even in traditions linked to particular places. As cities grow and land becomes more valuable, the pressure to replace older buildings with new ones increases. Supporters of development argue that change is necessary if places are to remain economically active. However, those who work in conservation point out that once a site is lost, the connection it offers to earlier generations cannot simply be rebuilt.

For a long time, heritage protection was mainly about freezing places in time. The aim was to restore damaged buildings so that they looked as they had in the past, while modern additions were kept out of sight. That approach still has value, but many specialists now prefer a broader view. They argue that historic areas should continue to be used rather than treated like stage sets. A former warehouse might become a library, for example, or a disused station could be turned into a market. According to this way of thinking, a building survives best when it remains part of daily life, even if that means accepting careful changes.

This idea can be difficult for local residents to accept at first. Some fear that popular heritage projects will attract tourists, raise prices and push out the people who have lived nearby for years. Others worry that once a site starts earning money, decisions will be driven more by business than by respect for history. Such concerns are understandable. There have been cases in which traditional neighbourhoods were renovated so thoroughly that they ended up looking neat but strangely empty, with souvenir shops replacing the communities that had given the area its identity. Preserving walls while losing real life is, in a sense, another kind of destruction.

Even so, refusing all change brings problems of its own. Historic buildings are expensive to maintain, and public funding is often limited. If no practical use can be found for an old structure, it may simply stand unused until its condition becomes dangerous. In that situation, calls to save it usually come too late. Conservationists therefore face a balancing act: they must protect the character of a place while allowing it to adapt enough to survive. Success often depends less on finding a perfect solution than on involving local people early, explaining proposed changes clearly and being honest about what cannot be preserved.

Technology is beginning to help with this process in unexpected ways. Digital mapping, 3D scanning and virtual models can record fragile sites in remarkable detail before repairs begin. These tools are not a substitute for the original, but they can guide restoration work and make collections accessible to people who may never travel to see them. Some experts are enthusiastic about these possibilities, while others warn that a virtual visit should not be confused with direct experience. Looking at a screen cannot reproduce the scale of a stone staircase or the smell of timber in an old theatre. Still, digital records may prove invaluable when disasters such as fire, flood or war damage places beyond immediate repair.

In the end, heritage is not just about age. It is about what communities decide is worth carrying forward. That judgment may involve beauty, memory, craftsmanship or the stories people attach to a site. The strongest preservation projects recognise that the past is neither untouchable nor endlessly reusable. Instead, they treat it as a shared resource that needs care, imagination and, above all, public trust. Without that trust, even well-funded schemes can fail. With it, preserving historical heritage becomes less an effort to resist time and more a way of giving the past a meaningful future.

questions.prompt: What point does the writer make in the opening paragraph?
options: A) Protecting heritage mainly means saving the most famous monuments.
B) Economic growth and heritage protection are always impossible to combine.
C) Heritage includes everyday places as well as well-known historic sites.
D) Most towns fail to recognise the value of their local traditions.
questions.evidence: The writer says heritage is found not only in famous landmarks but also in ordinary streets, workshops, archives and traditions linked to places.
questions.rationale: C is correct because the paragraph broadens the idea of heritage beyond major monuments. A is the opposite of the writer's point. B overstates the tension between development and conservation by saying they are always incompatible. D goes beyond the text, which mentions pressure on heritage but does not claim most towns fail to value it.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer mention turning a warehouse into a library and a station into a market?
options: A) To illustrate how historic buildings can remain useful through adapted reuse.
B) To suggest that public buildings are easier to preserve than private ones.
C) To show that modern architecture can improve neglected neighbourhoods.
D) To argue that restoration should hide all signs of contemporary change.
questions.evidence: The second paragraph explains that many specialists want historic areas to continue to be used and gives these examples to show buildings surviving as part of daily life.
questions.rationale: A is correct because the examples support the idea of giving old buildings new functions. B is unsupported; the text does not compare public and private preservation. C shifts the focus to modern architecture, which is not the point. D contradicts the paragraph, which accepts careful change rather than hiding all modern additions.

questions.prompt: What is suggested by the phrase 'another kind of destruction' in the third paragraph?
options: A) Physical damage is less serious than poor planning.
B) Renovation can harm heritage if it removes the life that made a place meaningful.
C) Tourism should be prevented in all traditional neighbourhoods.
D) Local residents are usually unwilling to support conservation work.
questions.evidence: The writer describes renovated areas becoming neat but empty, with souvenir shops replacing communities, and says preserving walls while losing real life is another kind of destruction.
questions.rationale: B is correct because the phrase refers to losing a place's living character even if its buildings remain. A creates a comparison the writer does not make. C is too absolute; the writer warns about some effects of tourism, not tourism itself in every case. D misreads the paragraph, which says residents' concerns are understandable, not that they usually oppose conservation.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's attitude towards change in historic buildings?
options: A) Strongly critical, because changes usually weaken a building's character.
B) Uncertain, because there is still not enough evidence to judge the results.
C) Supportive only when changes are invisible to the public.
D) Generally accepting, provided it helps survival without ignoring what matters about the place.
questions.evidence: The fourth paragraph says refusing all change causes problems and that conservationists must protect character while allowing enough adaptation for survival.
questions.rationale: D is correct because the writer presents change as necessary but says it must be managed carefully. A is too negative and ignores the argument for adaptation. B is inaccurate because the writer clearly takes a position. C reflects an older approach mentioned earlier, not the writer's overall view.

questions.prompt: What limitation of digital technology does the writer emphasise?
options: A) It is too expensive for most conservation projects to use regularly.
B) It cannot fully replace the experience of being at the real site.
C) It often produces records that are unreliable after disasters.
D) It encourages experts to ignore the opinions of local communities.
questions.evidence: The fifth paragraph says virtual models are not a substitute for the original and that a screen cannot reproduce the scale or smell of an old place.
questions.rationale: B is correct because the writer stresses the difference between digital access and direct experience. A is not mentioned. C distorts the point: digital records may actually help after disasters. D introduces an issue not linked to the discussion of technology.

questions.prompt: Which statement best sums up the writer's overall message?
options: A) Heritage survives best when experts are free to make difficult decisions quickly.
B) The main aim of preservation should be to recreate the past as accurately as possible.
C) Successful preservation depends on combining care for the past with practical use and public confidence.
D) New technology will soon solve the biggest problems facing historic sites.
questions.evidence: The final paragraph says strong projects treat heritage as a shared resource needing care, imagination and public trust, giving the past a meaningful future.
questions.rationale: C is correct because it reflects the article's central balance between protection, adaptation and trust. A overemphasises expert control and ignores community involvement. B repeats an outdated idea the article questions. D exaggerates the role of technology, which the writer presents as useful but limited.

6.title: Working With the Machine
6.passage:
A few years ago, stories about artificial intelligence at work usually focused on robots replacing people. The reality in many offices has turned out to be less dramatic, but in some ways more surprising. AI systems are now booking meetings, summarising reports and sorting customer emails before a human even sees them. (37) As a result, discussions about the future of work have become more practical, with managers and employees asking what should be automated and what should remain firmly in human hands.

One reason for this change is that the latest tools are easy to access. In the past, only large firms with specialist teams could afford to experiment with advanced software. Now even small businesses can pay for online services that write advertising copy, analyse sales figures or help staff organise their day. (38) Instead, they are often built into familiar workplace platforms, which means people start using them almost without noticing.

That quiet arrival can bring clear advantages. In hospitals, for example, AI can organise patient information so doctors spend less time on paperwork. In law firms, it can search huge collections of documents far faster than junior staff. (39) When routine tasks disappear, workers often have more time for decisions that require judgement, experience and direct contact with other people.

However, the same technology also creates new pressure. If a machine can produce a first draft of a report in seconds, employers may expect staff to complete more work in less time. Some workers say they now spend part of the day checking AI-generated material rather than producing their own. (40) In other words, efficiency does not always feel like freedom from the employee's point of view.

There is also the question of trust. AI tools are impressive, but they still make mistakes, and those mistakes can be hard to spot because the language they produce sounds confident. A chatbot may invent a source, while an image system might create misleading visual details. (41) For that reason, companies are increasingly training staff not just to use AI, but to question it carefully.

Another issue is what happens to workplace skills over time. If software always writes the first version of an email or presentation, younger employees may have fewer chances to develop those abilities themselves. Some experts worry this could weaken the very talents businesses will continue to need. (42) The challenge, then, is not simply to save time today, but to make sure tomorrow's workforce still knows how to think, write and solve problems independently.

For now, most evidence suggests that AI is changing jobs more often than it is eliminating them. New roles are appearing for people who can train systems, review outputs and decide when automation is useful. At the same time, older roles are being reshaped rather than wiped out completely. The workplace of the future may include more machines, but success will still depend on people knowing when to rely on them and when to switch them off.
sentencePool: A) Yet this shift has not removed work so much as altered the kind of work people do.
B) For that reason, some employers deliberately keep junior staff involved in first drafts and routine problem-solving, even when AI could do the work faster.
C) These tools do not usually arrive as dramatic new machines in the corner of the room.
D) This can mean the pace increases even when the task itself seems easier.
E) That is helpful only if professionals remain able to judge whether the results are accurate and relevant.
F) In creative industries, meanwhile, it can generate ideas quickly enough to help teams get started.
G) Some businesses have responded by banning personal phones during the working day.

7.partTitle: B2 Reading and Use of English Part 7: Multiple matching
7.directions: Read the article in which people talk about their experiences. For each question, choose from the people (A–D). The people may be chosen more than once.
7.matchingIntro: Which person…? The people may be chosen more than once.

sections.name: Leonie Marsh
sections.text: I started travelling alone almost by accident after a friend pulled out of a walking holiday in Portugal. Initially, I was annoyed rather than excited, but once I arrived, I realised how much easier it was to follow my own rhythm. If I wanted to spend three hours sketching in a fishing village, nobody minded. That freedom soon became the main attraction. However, I did discover that solo travel demands more practical effort than going away with company. When a train was cancelled, for instance, there was no one to compare ideas with, so every decision felt heavier. Since then, I have become far more organised before setting off. I still enjoy chatting to strangers in cafés and hostels, yet I do not travel alone in order to meet people. For me, the real benefit is having enough quiet time to notice places properly.

sections.name: Rafiq Siddons
sections.text: For years I avoided solo trips because I assumed they would feel lonely. Meanwhile, most of my friends were posting photographs from group holidays that looked far more entertaining. Then work sent me to Helsinki for a conference, and I added a few extra days on my own. To my surprise, being alone made me more approachable. In a group, I tend to stay with the people I know, whereas this time I ended up sharing meals with locals and other visitors. Not every moment was comfortable: one wet Sunday afternoon, I seriously considered booking an earlier flight home because the city seemed to empty out. Yet that brief low point taught me something useful. If you keep moving, even just to a gallery or market, the mood usually changes. I now plan at least one solo break each year, mainly because it pushes me beyond familiar habits.

sections.name: Marta Villiers
sections.text: My first independent journey came after a difficult year when I needed distance from everyday routines. I chose a rail pass and spent two weeks crossing central Europe with no detailed schedule. Friends described this as brave, but I saw it differently: travelling alone meant I did not have to negotiate every stop or justify changing my mind. Even so, the complete lack of structure was not as relaxing as I had imagined. After missing a connection in Prague, I found myself wishing I had booked at least the first few nights in advance. Since then, I have kept the spirit of flexibility while building in a framework. I reserve accommodation for the start of a trip, then leave room for last-minute choices later on. That balance suits me. I still return home refreshed, but I no longer confuse spontaneity with good planning.

sections.name: Noah Kerr
sections.text: Unlike some solo travellers, I did not set off in search of freedom or self-discovery. My reason was simpler: my partner hates long train journeys and museums, both of which I love. Rather than arguing over holiday plans, we sometimes travel separately for short periods. At first, I worried that people would assume I was alone because something had gone wrong in my life. In reality, the experience felt perfectly ordinary once I got used to eating dinner by myself. What I value most is the chance to become deeply absorbed in one subject. On a recent trip to northern Italy, I spent an entire day comparing small railway museums, which would have bored most of my friends. That said, I am not interested in proving I can manage everything independently. If a local guide offers expertise, I am happy to join a tour and learn more.
